intro: Five long reads: how origins-of-life research moved past its feuds, the Brazilian movement that built its own political machine, Europe's young in revolt against their elders, three ways businesses defy straight-line thinking, and why David's throne rested on loyal mercy.

stories.headline: Life's origin researchers stop fighting over one molecule
stories.dek: After decades of feuding over which molecule came first, origins-of-life research is turning to networks, functions and the possibility that life began more than once.
body: Some 4.6 billion years ago the solar system formed, and for a long while afterwards the Earth was molten and pelted by debris. Roughly 300 million years in, conditions settled enough for molecules to fall into loops that sustained and copied themselves. Over vast stretches of time those loops became cells, and the cells eventually became creatures able to wonder where they came from. By the mid-20th century science had made that wonder testable.

Testing, however, produced more hypotheses than answers. In a long feature for Quanta Magazine's origins-of-life package, Yasemin Saplakoglu describes a field that spent decades split into rival camps, each convinced that it had found the one molecule or the one setting where biology began. Some researchers spoke of a crisis; Betül Kaçar of the University of Wisconsin–Madison notes that crises are when breakthroughs happen.

Saplakoglu's argument is that a breakthrough of a kind is under way, though not the kind anyone expected. A younger generation has largely stopped asking which molecule came first. It is studying networks of molecules, the functions living systems perform and the chance that life arose more than once, and it is joining bottom-up chemistry to top-down evidence from genomes and, eventually, from other worlds.
## Rival worlds

The story starts with a prediction. In 1924 the Soviet biochemist Alexander Oparin forecast that chemists and biologists would one day meet in the middle. In 1952 Stanley Miller, a 23-year-old graduate student at the University of Chicago inspired by a lecture from Harold Urey, sealed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen in glassware, added sparks and a condenser to mimic rain, and produced five amino acids.

After Watson and Crick described DNA in 1953, attention swung to genetics. David Baum of Wisconsin–Madison says the field became “so obsessed” with genes. Researchers assumed that if they found which of a cell's three core features (genome, metabolism or compartment) came first, the rest would follow.

That assumption produced the rival “worlds”. The RNA world, which Matthew Powner of University College London calls the classic case of picking one molecule as first, gained ground after Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman showed in the 1980s that RNA can act as an enzyme, work that earned a Nobel prize. In 1988 Günter Wächtershäuser proposed an iron-sulphur world at hydrothermal vents, and Stuart Kauffman popularised self-sustaining “autocatalytic sets”, which fed metabolism-first ideas. Lipid, peptide, zinc and clay worlds followed, along with fights over location. Aaron Goldman of Oberlin College notes that each idea tended to be presented as the only correct one.
## From crisis to a thousand flowers

By the early 2000s, conferences could be hostile. Michael Travisano of the University of Minnesota recalls “unbelievable bickering”, and some professors discouraged students from talking to rival labs. The feud lasted because members were trained in different disciplines, because, as John Sutherland of the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology puts it, every camp had a valid point, and because no single-molecule system could be made to copy or sustain itself.

Then the problem changed shape. By the early 2010s it was clear that many building blocks, including sugars, nucleobases and fatty acids, can form under plausible early-Earth conditions. Meteorites such as Murchison, which fell in Australia in 1969, and Murray, which exploded over Kentucky in 1950, carried amino acids and some nucleobases. Cole Mathis of Arizona State University sums up the shift: the question moved from “How do we make anything?” to “How do we not make everything?”

A generational change helped. Joana Xavier and Mathis co-founded the Origin of Life Early-Career Network in 2020, and the article describes its members as less territorial than their predecessors. Joanna Masel of the University of Arizona entertains multiple origins. Gerald Joyce of the Salk Institute's phrase for the mood: let a thousand flowers bloom.
## Working backwards from LUCA

The second strand works from the other end. The last universal common ancestor, LUCA, was named in the 1990s. It left no fossils, but genomes preserve its traces; Greg Fournier of MIT calls genomes one of the two records of past life, alongside rocks. The oldest uncontested fossils are about 3.5 billion years old.

In 2024 Phil Donoghue's team at the University of Bristol estimated that LUCA had about 2,600 proteins, a genome comparable to modern bacteria, a basic metabolism, a membrane and a primitive immune system, and dated its lineage to roughly 4.2 billion years ago. If the planet became habitable around 4.4 billion years ago, LUCA appeared quickly. The team also found signs, in the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, that LUCA lived within a community of cells. So complex an ancestor means much of life's history predates it, a window Klára Hlouchová of Charles University in Prague calls the most exciting and the hardest to study.

Some of LUCA's genes were duplicated before LUCA existed. Goldman reconstructs early versions of proteins involved in electron transport, and Laurie Barge and Jessica Weber at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory test whether vent-like minerals interact with them to produce similar chemistry. Even success, Saplakoglu cautions, would not prove the pathway arose that way. Hlouchová's lab used AI-based protein design to show that a reduced alphabet of 10 amino acids can support the most conserved protein folds, and found that six amino acids identified in samples from the asteroid Bennu could produce many folds.
## Function over ingredients

A third strand asks what life does rather than what it is made of. Sijbren Otto of the University of Groningen argues the field has fixated on the molecules modern life happens to use. In 2010 his lab showed that synthetic stacks of benzene rings can copy themselves, preserving size-based information. Later they catalysed the making of their own precursors, and unpublished work reports “benzene cells” that grow and divide. They cannot yet evolve. Otto sees the passage from chemistry to life as a continuum with no sharp line, and Saplakoglu identifies evolution as the thread connecting all the strands.

The closest approach so far comes from Kate Adamala's team at the University of Minnesota, which packed liposomes with a DNA replication system, 36 enzymes and other components. Over months the vesicles grew, divided and showed a crude form of selection that the team calls a “poor man's evolution”. The July 2026 preprint uses highly evolved modern parts, so Adamala stresses it says nothing direct about life's origin. The cells cannot feed themselves. No one has yet built a self-sustaining, self-copying, independently evolving system.
## Looking elsewhere

The article ends by widening the frame. As Michael Lynch of Arizona State notes, a few decades of test tubes is little against the early Earth's few hundred million years. More than 6,000 exoplanets are known, perhaps 2,000 of them super-Earths, and ancient Mars and Saturn's moon Enceladus remain candidate habitats. NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory, planned for the 2040s, and ESA's Plato mission will search for biosignatures in planetary atmospheres. The field, Saplakoglu concludes, has one example of life to study. One day there could be two.

The caveats are substantial and the author states them: direct evidence of early life is minimal, LUCA reconstructions rest on methods still being refined, pre-LUCA chemistry is speculative, and the synthetic-cell result is an unreviewed preprint. Quanta also notes that several researchers quoted have Simons Foundation funding, the foundation that funds the magazine.
stories.counterpoint: Pluralism can be a polite word for a field that still lacks a decisive experiment. Letting a thousand flowers bloom avoids feuds, but it may also spread scarce funding across hypotheses that will never be tested, and a search for life elsewhere that depends on observatories planned for the 2040s defers the hard question rather than answering it.
stories.why: The origin of life is one of the few scientific questions that touches almost every discipline, from geochemistry to computing. The shift from rival dogmas to shared methods is also a case study in how a stuck research field gets unstuck, and the results will shape how future telescopes decide what counts as a sign of life.
questions: Is a field more likely to make progress when rival camps compete fiercely or when they cooperate, and what does this story suggest?
If life turned out to have begun more than once on Earth, would that change how you think about its place in the universe?
Where in your own work have you been arguing about which ingredient matters most when the real question was how the parts interact?

source.title: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
source.author: Yasemin Saplakoglu

stories.headline: Why Brazil's insurgents built their own machine
stories.dek: Oscar Campora argues that a movement wins lasting power only when it owns its money, ideas, media and people, and offers Brazil's Mission Party as the model.
body: The internet has made it cheap to reach millions of people. It has not made it any easier to turn that attention into durable political power. That, argues Oscar Campora, an Argentine-Brazilian political consultant based in São Paulo, remains as hard as it was when Lenin wrote What Is to Be Done. Reforming or refounding a state still requires an organisation whose members dedicate their lives to a shared goal, which survives both victory and defeat, and whose leaders keep evangelising when the cause is unpopular.

In a long essay for Palladium, Campora finds his example in an unlikely place. Brazil is usually cited abroad as a byword for inequality and dysfunctional politics. Yet he thinks one new party offers a lesson to anyone hoping to avoid “Brazilification” at home. Its central figure is Renan Santos, chairman of the Mission Party (Missão), leader of the Free Brazil Movement (MBL) and president of the magazine Valete.

Santos finished fourth in Brazil's 2026 presidential election. Campora concedes this was no triumph, though Santos beat two governors with more than eight years in office and nearly tied the third-place candidate. What matters more, he argues, is that the project survived and is already preparing for 2030.
## From Facebook event to impeachment

The movement began in 2014, after Aécio Neves, a former governor of Minas Gerais later linked to corruption scandals, lost the presidential race to Dilma Rousseff of the Workers' Party (PT). Renan Santos and his brother Alexandre, young São Paulo businessmen, set up a Facebook event whose slogan promised that either Dilma would fall or São Paulo would stop. About 100,000 people signed up, and thousands marched on November 1st.

The MBL's targets were the PT, in power since 2003, and the Centrão, a bloc of non-ideological political machines that trade congressional votes for public money. A commodities slowdown, the Operation Car Wash investigation into corruption at Petrobras and Rousseff's sliding popularity gave it momentum. Santos led members on a walk of more than 600 miles to Brasília, where they camped for months in the Three Powers Plaza. In April 2016, 367 of the 513 deputies in the Chamber voted to open impeachment proceedings; in August the Senate removed Rousseff.

Then, Campora says, the movement grew complacent. Jair Bolsonaro, a long-serving congressman and former army officer, claimed leadership of the right and won the 2018 election by a landslide. The MBL backed him in the run-off, but relations soured as he allied with Centrão politicians and, Campora writes, ran a large vote-buying operation through obscure budget channels, citing a Brazilian court ruling against the so-called secret budget.
## The cost of not owning a party

The deeper lesson concerns Brazil's rules. Its democracy is organised around parties rather than individuals; party funding is tied to congressional seats; independent candidacies are banned; and founding a party is expensive and slow. Bolsonaro changed parties ten times, and in 2021 his attempt to create the Alliance for Brazil collected 158,317 valid signatures against the 492,000 required. After 2022, Campora argues, Bolsonarismo dominated the right but could not reach the 50% needed to win, leaving what he calls a house with high floors and low ceilings.

The MBL learned the same lesson more painfully. In 2024 Kim Kataguiri, one of its members, sought the mayoralty of São Paulo, but his party, União Brasil, backed the incumbent, Ricardo Nunes. A movement without its own party, Campora concludes, is at the mercy of other people's calculations.

So it built one. Registering the Mission Party required 547,000 valid signatures spread across at least nine states with minimum quotas in each. According to Campora, the MBL gathered five times as many notarised signatures as Bolsonaro had managed. Victor Couto, the party's secretary-general, wrote custom software to manage the drive, and volunteers were ranked and rewarded in what Campora describes as gamification.
## Vertical integration

The organising principle is to keep everything in-house: ideas, activism, candidacies, media and social platforms. The party believes, Campora reports, that outsourcing leads to deradicalisation. For American readers he offers an analogy: imagine one executive controlling the Economic Policy Institute, the Democratic Socialists of America, Politico, Substack and the Democratic National Committee.

The ideas arm produced the Yellow Book, a 360-page governing programme for 2026 distilled from six research volumes by more than 200 volunteers. Among its proposals is a Managerial Responsibility Law that would allocate the federal Electoral Fund according to mayors' performance on infrastructure, sanitation and education, judged by an independent committee modelled on a central bank; underperforming mayors would lose money and their parties would be fined. Mayors could call on federal “forward deployed engineers” to help them hit targets. The book treats cartels as terrorists and proposes favela pacification and planned neighbourhoods, which Campora likens to Nayib Bukele's crackdown in El Salvador. Its economic agenda leans on agribusiness, the EMBRAPA research agency, rail and Shenzhen-style special economic zones; Campora cites agribusiness exports of $164 billion in 2024.

The personnel arm is Academia MBL, which sorts trainees into three “phalanxes”: Spartans for organisation, Alexandrians for policy and philosophy, Athenians for rhetoric and social media. Mixed teams take on local projects, completion is required before anyone runs a branch, and failure to meet guidelines means expulsion. The money arm is Valete, launched in January 2023 and described as Brazil's second-best-selling cultural publication, whose platform has more than 10,000 paying subscribers and helped finance the signature drive. Santos calls the arrangement a Holy Trinity: Valete for culture, the MBL for provocation, the party for institutional action.
## Becoming the centre of your world

Campora's prescription goes beyond Brazil. Movements should not settle for being one node in a loose network; they should aim to be a monopoly grounded in intellectual and technological superiority, generating their own funding, theory, media, activists and policy. Staff should be chosen for loyalty rather than public-sector experience. He invokes Antonio Gramsci's “organic cohesion”, a living bond between leaders and members that marries political understanding to popular passion, and describes Santos's daily livestreams as a funnel from casual viewer to subscriber to academy student to party leader, comparing their habit-forming pull to smoking.

He is candid about the limits. The party is still building its cadres, fourth place is a long way from power, and whether it succeeds depends on too many variables to forecast. But he ends with a firm claim: when Lula and Bolsonaro are gone, parties that outsource their functions will be beaten by vertically integrated ones.
stories.counterpoint: Campora is a consultant writing admiringly about a movement, and the essay offers little independent evidence that vertical integration wins elections rather than simply building loyal subcultures. An organisation that prizes loyalty over experience, expels members who miss guidelines and treats its leader's livestreams like a habit-forming product also carries obvious risks of insularity and personality cult.
stories.why: Across democracies, insurgent movements rise on online energy and then dissolve into existing parties or vanish. Brazil's experiment is a live test of whether owning the whole stack of money, ideas, media and training changes that pattern, and the answer matters to anyone trying to build, or to resist, a new political force.
questions: Is a movement that controls its own media, funding and training more durable, or simply more closed to correction?
Which of the Yellow Book's ideas, such as tying mayors' funding to performance, would you want tested where you live, and which worry you?
In the organisations you belong to, what functions are outsourced that perhaps should be owned, and what is owned that should be shared?

stories.headline: Europe's young are revolting against their elders
stories.dek: John Last argues that this autumn's protests in Italy and France are a revolt against a gerontocracy that holds the houses, the votes and the budget.
body: In Milan this autumn, soldiers with an average age of 38 arrested protesters, some as young as 12 or 13. Italy's government, whose members average 60, passed a decree allowing detention for up to 24 hours without charge and arrests of vandals up to 48 hours after the fact. Matteo Salvini, the 53-year-old deputy prime minister, proposed fining the parents of vandals. In late October protests reached at least a dozen Italian cities, and luxury shops in Milan were looted.

France, according to John Last, has had it worse: weeks of blocked city centres, smoke over Paris and 53 police officers injured in a single weekend. President Emmanuel Macron blamed radical far-left groups and criminals. The French protests began over a university application portal but spread to fuel prices, crowded schools, housing and insecure work. One Paris protester's summary, quoted in the essay, is that it has been too long and too much.

Last, a Canadian freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent who has also served as a union steward at Canada's public broadcaster, argues in Noema that these are not scattered riots. They are, he writes, one of the largest generational conflicts in decades: a revolt by the young against a gerontocracy of ageing baby-boomers who have accumulated the assets and political influence and passed the costs down.
## Who holds what

Last's case rests on a set of distributional figures. On his numbers, boomers, born between 1946 and 1964, own about a third of Italy's housing stock and receive about a quarter of French public spending, while in Spain, he writes, rent can consume 98% of an average salary. Boomers hold 28% of American family homes, by his count, and in Australia senior investment in rental property has risen by 1,500% while rents nearly doubled.

He traces the arrangement to the elder poverty of the 1920s and 1930s, which prompted states to build what Pieter Vanhuysse of the University of Southern Denmark calls “asymmetric socialisation”: the state looks after the old while families look after the young. Longer lives and low birth rates have since doubled the share of over-65s in France and Italy, to one in five and one in four residents respectively. The American median age has risen by ten years since 1960. The world has fewer than a billion people over 65, a number expected to double by 2060.
## Votes and budgets

Demography turns into politics through turnout. In France, Britain, Germany, America and other rich countries, people aged 65 and over are 10-20% more likely to vote than those aged 18 to 25. People under 30 make up half the world's population but hold about 2% of legislative seats, a “representational deficit” in the phrase of Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. Vanhuysse's research finds that nearly all the countries he surveyed tilt state spending towards the old.

France is Last's prime example. Its public debt exceeds its annual output. In Vanhuysse's index it ranks just behind Japan for the political power granted to the elderly, and he estimates that about $5 is spent on older citizens for every $1 spent on the young. Nearly two in five civil servants are over 50. Pensions absorb a quarter of public spending, including, Last writes, a third of the education ministry's budget, and the result shows up in crumbling schools and crowded universities. He cites Thomas Piketty's observation that France cut spending per student by 20% while never having been richer, with private wealth doubling relative to GDP; for Piketty the problem is simply one of distribution.
## A two-tier economy

Boomers, Last argues, entered work at the peak of unionisation, with stable jobs, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions, and bought starter homes for two or three years' income. The equivalent ratio today is nearly ten. Vanhuysse estimates that a working French person can expect lifetime wealth 17% below a boomer's, a gap he likens to the difference between raising two children and raising none.

Older voters, in Last's account, have resisted the obvious remedies: pension cuts, later retirement, rent controls, changes to capital-gains tax and new housing. In some places inequality is written into law. Italy, facing youth unemployment of 42%, allowed short-term contracts only for workers hired after 2014; today 40% of workers under 29 are in precarious jobs, against 5% of those over 50. Last recognises the pattern from his own workplace, where established staff had secure pensions and young temporary workers had none. Artificial intelligence, harder hiring tests and constant economic disruption add to the pressure. He also points to schools: 10% of teaching hours in France go untaught because of chronic absence, and he questions whether the time parents give children, which Vanhuysse values at up to seven months' wages a year, means much when many children were left alone with screens.
## Repression and nihilism

Stockemer describes a vicious cycle of alienation: politicians serve older voters, the young disengage, and governments respond even less. Giorgia Meloni's government has banned raves, lowered the age of criminal responsibility and increased juvenile detention by 50%. A statement from the October 17 Movement, one of the Italian protest organisers, rejects a government that answers with soldiers, handcuffs and decrees.

Last does not cast the old simply as villains. Boomers turning 65 before 2030 can expect about 20 more years of life; high housing costs stop them downsizing, inflation erodes benefits and home care in Europe costs over $1,000 a month. The great wealth transfer of more than $100 trillion is, he argues, being diverted to health-care companies. The petty landlord, the retiring civil servant and the looting teenager are, in his phrase, dogs fighting for scraps, and he sees new alliances forming among students, lorry drivers, migrants and middle-class couples.

He contrasts today's protesters with earlier waves, from the Red Army Faction and Brigate Rosse in the 1970s to French student protests in the 1980s and Italy's Pantera movement in the 1990s, which were arguably less desperate. Many of those arrested now have no criminal record and no faith in institutions. Last warns that opportunists, criminals and fascists may exploit the mood. Stockemer expects another outbreak of rage in two years. The essay closes bleakly: the young are growing more radical, and no pension will be generous enough to spare the old the consequences.
stories.counterpoint: Framing the problem as boomers against the young may misdiagnose it. Wealth within each generation is highly unequal, many pensioners are poor, and housing scarcity owes as much to planning rules and interest rates as to any cohort's selfishness; Last's own sources, including Piketty, point to distribution in general rather than age. Several of his figures are also contested or loosely defined.
stories.why: Ageing electorates are the norm across the rich world and much of Asia, so the fiscal and political pattern Last describes will not stay European. Whether governments answer it with housing supply, pension reform and youth representation, or with decrees and detention, will shape social stability for decades.
questions: Is generational conflict the right lens for these protests, or does it hide a more ordinary story about wealth and class?
What would a fair settlement between generations look like on housing and pensions where you live?
When have you seen an institution protect its established members at the expense of newcomers, and what did it cost the institution?

stories.headline: When a small stumble becomes a big fall
stories.dek: Polymath Investor warns that businesses rarely behave in straight lines, and that headline numbers can hide the mechanisms that matter.
body: Investors like straight lines. A business whose numbers tell a clear story, whose next year looks much like its last, is what Warren Buffett called a one-foot hurdle: a situation in which you do not need to be especially clever to see what comes next. Most businesses, unfortunately, are not like that.

In a new essay, the first of a promised series, the pseudonymous author of the Polymath Investor newsletter names the error of assuming otherwise. A “linearity trap”, the author writes, is the habit of assuming that a business behaves in simple, proportional ways when in reality its profits, risks, competitive advantages and valuation can change in sudden and counterintuitive ones. The author notes a cousin of the idea in data science, “linearity bias”: the tendency to expect relationships and trends to continue in a straight line even when the underlying system behaves differently.

The point, the essay argues, is that these dynamics are rarely visible in the financial statements alone. Understanding a business is not the same as analysing its accounts. You still have to do the work of learning the cause-and-effect relationships that drive its economics.
## Why this matters more now

The author ties the argument to the rush into artificial intelligence. As AI gets better at processing information, crunching numbers and spotting patterns, purely quantitative strategies are likely to face more intense competition, the essay suggests. If every fund can screen the same ratios instantly, the edge from reading the numbers shrinks. The more durable advantage, on this view, belongs to fundamental investors who understand why a business behaves as it does, rather than merely observing what the figures show. That is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result, but it frames the three examples that follow.
## Risk is not proportional

The first example concerns leverage. Imagine a company with $100m of debt that earns about $15m a year, and suppose its earnings fall by 10%. Linear intuition says the business is now 10% worse off: unwelcome, but hardly a catastrophe.

Not necessarily, says the author. A modest decline could push the company into breaching a debt covenant, one of the conditions lenders attach to a loan. At that point the situation changes in kind rather than degree. Lenders may gain the right to demand immediate repayment. Refinancing becomes far more expensive, if it is possible at all. Shareholders may suffer heavy dilution if the company is forced to issue new shares on painful terms, and in extreme cases the firm may end up in bankruptcy.

The essay's arithmetic is stark: under the wrong circumstances, a 10% fall in earnings can wipe out 80% of a stock's value. The author is careful to say this depends on how leveraged the company is and how its debt agreements are written, and that most businesses will not suffer anything so dramatic from a modest dip. But that is precisely the point. The size of the fall bears no fixed relation to the size of the stumble. What turns one into the other is a threshold buried in a loan agreement, which no growth rate or margin on the income statement will reveal.
## More capacity, less output

The second example runs against the instinct that investment equals growth. More spending, more capacity, more output: it sounds logical. Yet expanding a business can sometimes make it less efficient.

The author imagines a shipping company with 100 lorries whose loading docks and warehouses already run near capacity. Management adds 30 more lorries to raise revenue. But the extra vehicles cause congestion at the docks, longer waits and higher operating costs, and the firm may end up delivering fewer parcels per hour than before. Thirty new lorries, and a less productive operation.

The general principle is familiar to anyone who has studied operations: the output of a system is governed by its tightest constraint, and adding resources anywhere else can simply lengthen the queue in front of it. The author concedes that one would expect management to anticipate such bottlenecks before committing capital, and adds, drily, that in reality this does not always happen. For an investor, the lesson is that a rising capital-expenditure line is not evidence of growth until you know where the constraint sits.
## Every division worse, the company better
The third example is the most striking. Can a company's overall performance improve while every one of its divisions deteriorates? It sounds like a contradiction, but the essay supplies numbers.

Take a firm with two divisions. The high-margin one earned a 40% profit margin last year and 35% this year. The low-margin one went from 10% to 8%. Both are getting worse. Yet the company's overall margin jumped from 16% to 29.6%. The explanation is the mix. Last year the high-margin division supplied only 20% of revenue; this year it supplied 80%. The figures check out: 20% of revenue at 40% plus 80% at 10% gives 16%, while 80% at 35% plus 20% at 8% gives 29.6%.

This is an instance of Simpson's paradox, in which a trend that holds within every group reverses when the groups are combined, because their relative weights have changed. The author leaves open whether such a company is becoming a better business or a worse one. A shift towards the more profitable division is good news, but the underlying profitability of both units is eroding, and anyone reading only the consolidated accounts would miss it. Aggregates, the essay concludes, can hide exactly what an investor ought to be examining.
## Better questions

What should analysts ask instead? Headline metrics such as revenue growth, margins and valuation ratios still matter, the author says, but they rarely tell the whole story. The most interesting questions are often those where the intuitive answer turns out to be wrong. Rather than asking whether a number is rising or falling, ask why it is changing, which forces drive it, and under what circumstances an apparent improvement could be a warning sign.

The essay's conclusion is that escaping the trap means treating a company's numbers as the start of an investigation rather than its end. Some of the best opportunities come from understanding how a business actually works rather than extrapolating from its statements. In investing, the author writes, the shortest distance between two points is not always a straight line.
stories.counterpoint: None of the three examples is new to a trained analyst: covenant risk, operational bottlenecks and mix effects are standard fare in credit analysis and segment reporting, and the essay uses stylised numbers rather than real companies. Its claim that AI will erode quantitative strategies while sparing fundamental judgement is also untested; the same tools may soon read loan agreements and segment notes faster than any human.
stories.why: Most investing mistakes come not from missing data but from misreading what the data imply. A short checklist built from these three traps, namely where are the thresholds, where is the constraint and what is the mix, is a cheap defence against extrapolating a headline number into a costly decision.
questions: Which company you follow could lose far more than a proportional amount from a modest fall in earnings, and why?
When has adding resources to a project made it slower rather than faster in your own experience?
What aggregate figure in your organisation might be hiding a decline in every part that makes it up?

stories.headline: David's throne rested on hesed, not force
stories.dek: Peter Leithart reads 1–2 Samuel as a realist account of power in which David's claim to be a king after God's heart rests on loyal mercy rather than strength.
body: Ask most readers what made David a great king and they will reach for the sling and the stone. The popular picture is of a warrior: the boy who felled Goliath, the commander whose thousands outnumbered Saul's. Peter Leithart, president of the Theopolis Institute, thinks that picture misses what the books of Samuel are actually saying about power.

In a short exegetical essay for First Things, Leithart argues that Samuel and Kings offer a realistic portrait of political rule, neither naive nor cynical, and that the story of David shows rule finding its proper shape in hesed, the Hebrew word usually rendered lovingkindness or steadfast love. Hesed is the word Scripture uses for God's covenant faithfulness to Israel. When a king displays it, Leithart suggests, he is mirroring the character of the God who appointed him.
The essay moves between two poles that the books themselves set up: a warning about what kings do, and a vision of what a king could be.
## Two pictures of a king

The first pole is 1 Samuel 8. Israel asks for a king like the nations around it, and Samuel warns what such a king will take: their fields and property, a tenth of their produce, their sons for his chariots and armies, and their daughters for his court. God grants the request anyway. Leithart draws attention to the irony of the warning and to the detail of the daughters taken into royal service, a reminder that power in the ancient world, as now, extracts from the vulnerable first.

The second pole is 2 Samuel 23, David's last words. There the righteous ruler who governs in the fear of God is like morning light after rain, making the grass spring from the earth. Leithart notes the double edge of the image. The people are grass, which is transient, yet they are also the king's pasture, something he exists to nourish. The ideal king feeds his people and brings hidden evil into the light.

Neither picture, Leithart observes, fully describes the two kings who dominate 1–2 Samuel. Saul begins well but is consumed by envy of David; his story ends with a visit to a medium and death by his own hand on Mount Gilboa. David is far from spotless, yet the narrative still calls him a man after God's own heart. That, Leithart suggests, means God's approval rests on virtues other than the ones we might expect.
## Loyalty to an enemy

The first of those virtues is loyalty to someone who is trying to kill you. Saul hunts David for years, yet David serves him faithfully. Even in exile among the Philistines, Leithart notes, David fights Saul's enemies, and when he has the chance to kill Saul he refuses to take revenge. Readers will recall the cave at En Gedi and the camp where David takes Saul's spear and water jug but leaves the king asleep.

Leithart reads these episodes as an illustration, long before the New Testament, of the Pauline command not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good. He also sees the Beatitudes operating politically: the meek David inherits the land and the throne. The man who would not seize the kingdom is the one to whom it is given.
## Mourning the fallen

The second virtue is grief for enemies. When Saul and Jonathan die, David composes a lament for them both. When Joab murders Abner, Saul's general, David mourns him publicly and follows the bier. Leithart argues these acts do two things at once. They demonstrate David's innocence of the deaths, which matters for a man whose rise benefits from them, and they begin to heal the rivalry between the tribes loyal to Saul's house and those loyal to David. Leithart reads them as a political form of Jesus's command to love one's enemies and do good to those who mistreat you.
## Mephibosheth at the table

The essay's central example is Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, who is lame in both feet. As the surviving heir of Saul's line he is a potential rallying point for the old regime, and ancient political prudence would counsel removing him. David does the opposite. He restores Saul's land to him and gives him a permanent place at the king's table. The narrator calls this hesed, and Leithart stresses the echo: the same word names God's steadfast love for Israel and David's covenant loyalty to Jonathan. What would have been a liability under realpolitik becomes, in David's court, an act that images God.
## Where mercy fails

Leithart does not offer a hagiography. He insists that David's mercy sometimes curdles into something destructive. After his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, David fails to restrain his sons, and his household falls into incest, murder and rebellion. When Absalom revolts, David is so gentle with him that Joab rebukes the king sharply. Joab himself becomes a serial killer within the court, murdering Abner and later Amasa, and eventually joins Adonijah's attempted coup against Solomon. David's dying instruction to Solomon to deal with Joab, Leithart notes, comes far too late; it would have been wiser had David acted earlier.

The failures matter to the argument. They show that hesed is not mere softness or a refusal to judge. The model Leithart points to is the Lord's self-description to Moses on Sinai, the confession of a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, who nonetheless will by no means clear the guilty. David partly embodies that combination. Where he holds mercy and justice together, his reign flourishes; where mercy slips its moorings from justice, his house collapses.
## The king after God's heart

Leithart's conclusion is that the swashbuckling David of popular imagination is the wrong lesson from Samuel. The books are realist about power, frank about what kings take and how often they fail. But their portrait of a good ruler is not someone who wields force most effectively. It is someone whose loyalty survives betrayal, who mourns his enemies and who sets a place at his table for the heir of a rival house. That combination of mercy and justice, rather than strength, is what makes David a king after God's own heart.
stories.counterpoint: A critic could say Leithart reads the David story too charitably. Many scholars see the narratives of David's grief over Saul, Abner and others as royal apologetic, written to clear a usurper of suspicion, and the same David who spared Saul later arranged Uriah's death and left Joab's violence unchecked for decades. Mercy that is selectively applied to political advantage may be prudence rather than hesed.
stories.why: The essay gives preachers a way to teach 1–2 Samuel that resists both hero worship and cynicism: David's greatness lies in covenant loyalty, not prowess, and his failures show what happens when mercy is cut loose from justice. Mephibosheth at the king's table is also a natural bridge to the gospel's picture of the undeserving welcomed by grace, and to Christian leadership that refuses to secure power by eliminating rivals.
questions: Where are you tempted to secure your position by removing a rival rather than showing them loyal kindness?
How can mercy be extended without becoming the permissiveness that let Absalom and Joab run unchecked?
Who in your life is a Mephibosheth, someone with a claim on your kindness only because of a covenant made with another?

recall.headline: The boulder you keep leaving halfway up the hill
recall.dek: Most of what compounds in a life is lost not to failure but to interruption, and the remedy is less heroic than we would like.
body: Look at the last three things you started with real enthusiasm. A morning run, perhaps, or a language app, or a journal. Each began with a burst: new shoes, a streak, three pages on the first night. Now ask where each one stands. If you are like most people, at least one is not finished and not abandoned either. It is simply paused, waiting for a better month.

That pause is the subject of this essay. It is easy to treat it as harmless, since nothing was lost and you can always resume. Two sources suggest the opposite: that the pause is where most of the value in a life quietly drains away, and that the people who seem unusually capable are often distinguished less by talent than by their refusal to pause.
## Three buckets, one answer

The first source is a talk by the investor Peter Kaufman, retold by Shane Parrish on The Knowledge Project's Outliers series. Kaufman's method for finding ideas he could trust was to test them against the largest relevant samples he could think of. He called them three buckets: roughly 13.7 billion years of the inorganic universe, about 3.5 billion years of life on Earth, and some 20,000 years of recorded human history. A principle that holds in all three, he argued, is about as reliable as principles get.

One question he put to the buckets was what the most powerful force is that a person can harness. In finance the answer is compound interest. In biology it is evolution. In human achievement it is the slow accumulation behind an Olympic medal, a mastered instrument, a learned language or a business like Berkshire Hathaway. Kaufman's definition covers all three: dogged, incremental, constant progress over a long period of time.

The definition matters because of its middle word. Kaufman's claim, as Parrish tells it, is that people do not fail to compound because they misunderstand the maths. Most of us can explain compounding to a teenager. We fail because we hate being constant. His image is a self-made Sisyphus: we push the boulder halfway up the hill, decide to come back to it next month, and watch it roll down. Every interruption knocks us off the exponential curve and back onto a linear one, or below it. Asked how Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger got rich, Kaufman's answer was that they were constant, not intermittent. Parrish draws the lesson plainly: intensity is overrated and consistency is underrated.
## Most people quit; few fail

The second source comes from a very different world. On the Modern Wisdom podcast, the retired general Stanley McChrystal described his first two years at West Point as close to disastrous, with low grades, a punishment for disrespect towards a superior and two serious disciplinary cases involving alcohol, the second within a day of finishing the first. He was nearly expelled.

Decades later, he defines self-discipline simply as the ability to get yourself to do what you have decided you should do, especially when tired or angry, and calls it the gap between good leaders and everyone else. His most striking evidence concerns elite military selection. People imagine Rangers, SEALs and Delta operators as physically superhuman, he said, but the entry standards are not that high. Of those who start the nine-week Ranger course, by his rough estimate perhaps 35 to 40% earn the tab and maybe 5% fail outright. The rest decide to stop. The selection process, in his account, is designed to find out who will not quit, because that is the trait that matters later.
## The synthesis

Put the two together and a pattern appears, though the connection is this essay's, not either speaker's. Kaufman says the returns in a life come from constancy. McChrystal says the people who reach the hardest goals are mostly those who did not stop. Both are describing the same hidden variable. Outcomes that look like differences in ability are frequently differences in interruption.

That reframing is useful because it moves attention away from the moment we tend to obsess over, the heroic start, towards the moment we neglect: the first missed day. The start feels decisive because it is vivid. But compounding is indifferent to how dramatically something began. It cares only whether the line was broken. A modest habit kept for three years will usually beat an intense one kept for three weeks and restarted four times. The arithmetic of a broken line is unforgiving: each restart begins near the bottom of the curve, where progress is slowest and motivation is most needed, so the person who keeps restarting spends most of their effort in the least rewarding stretch.

It also suggests that quitting is rarely one decision. McChrystal's candidates did not, for the most part, fail a test; they chose to stop. In ordinary life the choice is even quieter. Nobody announces that the journal is finished. It is postponed until after a busy week, and then again. The pause is the quitting, disguised as a delay.

There is a caution worth adding. Constancy is not the same as rigidity, and McChrystal concedes in the same conversation that stubbornness and pride can look a great deal like discipline. Being constant at the wrong thing simply compounds the wrong thing. The question to ask is not only whether you kept going, but whether the thing deserved to be kept.
## A practical test

Take the paused projects you counted at the start and apply one rule to each: shrink it until it can survive your worst week. If the run has stalled, the commitment becomes ten minutes, not five miles. If the language lapsed, the target becomes one lesson a day rather than an hour on Saturdays. Then write down what you will do on the day you miss, because you will miss one. The aim is not to make the effort impressive; it is to make the line unbroken. Kaufman's word was constant, and a small thing done constantly is still constant.
Three months from now, the test of this idea will not be whether you remember the three buckets or the Ranger statistics. It will be whether the boulder is higher up the hill than it is today.
questions: Which of your current projects is paused rather than finished, and what is the smallest version of it you could do every day starting this week?
sources: Peter D. Kaufman, The Multidisciplinary Approach to Thinking, retold by Shane Parrish on The Knowledge Project (Outliers series), approx. 0:06–0:15.
Stanley McChrystal with Chris Williamson, Modern Wisdom #942, How to Actually Build Discipline, approx. 0:00–0:16.
